system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- Evidence text comes from a PDF text layer. If symbols are garbled so that you cannot verify the atom, answer "hold" for that check and say so.
- Be strict. When unsure between pass and a non-pass value, choose the non-pass value and explain.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom. pass = fully stated. revise = the core claim is stated, and the gap is only wording, strength, or a dropped/extra peripheral qualifier that can be fixed by deleting or softening words (say what). fail = not stated, OR the atom adds substantive content the evidence lacks: a scope or population restriction (e.g. 'In B-ALL'), a mechanism or operation, a characterization (e.g. 'an unbounded while loop'), or a formula/definition. If deleting the unsupported part would change what the atom tests, it is fail, not revise. For pass, put the supporting evidence ids in cite (required).
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / revise / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge: one fact a person who studied the concept would simply know. revise = the core fact is recall-level but the sentence carries extra load that must be removed, e.g. stacked conditions (since/although/if ... and ...), a procedural or evaluative add-on ('easy to define but requires checking ...'), or a clause that introduces a second technical concept that must be known separately (e.g. 'if X is an inner Kan complex' when that is not the card concept). fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = the authors' opinion or choice, or the finding of one study, so the answer is not fixed without the source.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a single system, product, or one study's topic.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Knowledge Graph Management System
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: KGs viewed as management systems analogous to DBMSs: required services (add, derive, retrieve), the Bellomarini three-component definition (ground extensional, intensional, derived extensional), and the KGMS desiderata and Vadalog focus. Excludes application-service requirements.

ATOMS:
- KGBDP-C10-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Viewing a Knowledge Graph as a knowledge management system is analogous to a database management system for databases: a system to create, manipulate and retrieve data.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0035-s14] In this section, we present the view of Knowledge Graphs as knowledge management systems.
    [KGBDP-p0035-s15] The clear analogy to see here is what a database management system is for databases: A system to create, manipulate and retrieve data.
- KGBDP-C10-S1-02.r1a | S1
  ATOM: A knowledge graph can be defined as a semi-structured data model made up of three components: a ground extensional component, an intensional component, and a derived extensional component.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0035-s11] “A semi-structured datamodel characterized by three components: (i) a ground extensional component, that is, a set of relational constructs for schema and data (which can be effectively modeled as graphs or generalizations thereof); (ii) an intensional component, that is, a set of inference rules over the constructs of the ground extensional component; (iii) a derived extensional component that can be produced as the result of the application of the inference rules over the ground extensional component (with the so-called “reasoning” process).” – Bellomarini et al., 2019 – [40].
- KGBDP-C10-S1-02.r1b | S1
  ATOM: In this definition of a knowledge graph, the ground extensional component is a set of relational constructs for schema and data, which can be effectively modeled as graphs or generalizations thereof.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0035-s11] “A semi-structured datamodel characterized by three components: (i) a ground extensional component, that is, a set of relational constructs for schema and data (which can be effectively modeled as graphs or generalizations thereof); (ii) an intensional component, that is, a set of inference rules over the constructs of the ground extensional component; (iii) a derived extensional component that can be produced as the result of the application of the inference rules over the ground extensional component (with the so-called “reasoning” process).” – Bellomarini et al., 2019 – [40].
- KGBDP-C10-S1-02.r1c | S2
  ATOM: In this definition of a knowledge graph, the intensional component is a set of inference rules over the constructs of the ground extensional component, and the derived extensional component is produced by applying these rules to the ground extensional component through reasoning.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0035-s11] “A semi-structured datamodel characterized by three components: (i) a ground extensional component, that is, a set of relational constructs for schema and data (which can be effectively modeled as graphs or generalizations thereof); (ii) an intensional component, that is, a set of inference rules over the constructs of the ground extensional component; (iii) a derived extensional component that can be produced as the result of the application of the inference rules over the ground extensional component (with the so-called “reasoning” process).” – Bellomarini et al., 2019 – [40].
- KGBDP-C10-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: The management-system view adds to the knowledge-representation view the services that a Knowledge Graph as a knowledge management system has to offer.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0035-s16] What this adds to the previous section’s view of KGs as knowledge representation tools is the service that a KG as a knowledge management system has to offer.
- KGBDP-C10-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: The desiderata for a Knowledge Graph Management System include high expressive power (at least as expressive as Datalog, i.e., full recursion), ontological reasoning (at least as expressive as SPARQL and OWL 2 QL), and low complexity (a core language tractable in data complexity).
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0038-s10] The authors pose a number of requirements or desiderata for a Knowledge Graph Management System (KGMS) in terms of the main system capabilities:
    [KGBDP-p0038-s11] – simple modular syntax: easy to add and remove facts and rules – high expressive power: at least as expressive as Datalog (i.e., full recursion) – numeric computation and aggregation: real-world required features – ontological reasoning: at least as expressive as SPARQL and OWL 2 QL – probabilistic reasoning: should support a form of probabilistic reasoning – low complexity: the core language should be tractable in data complexity – rule repository, management and ontology editor: management facilities – dynamic orchestration: allow orchestration of complex, real-world workflows
- KGBDP-C10-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: A Knowledge Graph as a knowledge management system must support the user in adding knowledge to the KG, deriving new knowledge from existing knowledge, and retrieving data through a general-purpose query language.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0035-s17] In particular, it has to provide support for the user to (i) add knowledge to a KG (ii)
    [KGBDP-p0036-s01] derive new knowledge using existing knowledge, and (iii) retrieve data through a form of general-purpose query language.
- KGBDP-C10-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: The Vadalog system was presented in technical detail with a focus on algorithms and data structures that meet the requirements of high expressive power, ontological reasoning and low complexity at the same time.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0038-s15] They subsequently presented the Vadalog system [38] in more technical detail, focusing on algorithms and data structures to meet the requirement on high expressive power, ontological reasoning and low complexity at the same time.
- KGBDP-C10-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: The authors consider question answering and recommender system capabilities typically to be application services, whereas general-purpose services such as entity resolution and link prediction are less clear, since they could be seen as requirements of a general-purpose knowledge management system.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0039-s09] For example, while question answering in our opinion would typically be considered as an application service, as would be offering recommender system capabilities, it is less clear for relatively generalpurpose application services such as entity resolution and link prediction, which could be seen as a requirement of a general purporse knowledge management system.
- KGBDP-C10-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: The authors treat question answering, recommender systems, entity resolution and link prediction as application services because they offer a well-defined application, in contrast to a management system that offers a query language supporting such applications.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0039-s10] Here, we will consider all of four of these as application services as they clearly offer a well-defined application compared to a management system offering a query language that supports such applications.
- KGBDP-C10-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: The source states that the border between the management view and the application-service view of KGs is debatable, and invites readers to consider what counts as an essential general-purpose service of a knowledge management system versus an application service.
  EVIDENCE:
    [KGBDP-p0039-s07] Clearly, the border between the two views of management and application is debatable, and we invite the reader to critically think of what one should consider as an essential general-purpose service of a knowledge management system, and what should be part of an application service.
